Watch the accent on miércoles (MIÉR-co-les) and sábado (SÁ-ba-do).
GI is read like a harsh h: gimnasio = “heem-na-syo”.
Spaniards link words together: “a las ocho” sounds like “alasocho”, “me levanto” like “melevanto”. Listen and copy the rhythm.
The days are written with a small letter, unlike English. They are all masculine: el lunes, el martes…
The Spanish days come from the Latin names of the planets and gods — look how many you can recognise!
Don’t put “en” before the day: “El lunes voy al médico”, not “en lunes” (English “on Monday” has no equivalent preposition here).

The question: “¿Qué hora es?”. The answer uses SER: “Es la una” for 1 o’clock (una is singular), “Son las…” for all the other hours (dos, tres… are plural). The word “hora” is understood: “las dos” = “(the hours) two”.
The hour comes first, then the minutes: “quarter past” = y cuarto, “half past” = y media, “quarter to” = menos cuarto (literally “minus a quarter”).
At what time? = ¿A qué hora? → “A las ocho” (at eight), “A la una” (at one).
Reflexive verbs carry a small pronoun that refers back to the subject: “me levanto” = literally “I raise myself” = I get up. The pronoun goes before the verb.
Other useful reflexives: ducharse (to have a shower): me ducho; vestirse (to get dressed): me visto; acostarse (to go to bed): me acuesto.
In the dictionary you recognise a reflexive verb by the “-se” at the end: levantarSE, llamarSE. You already know one: “me llamo” = my name is (literally “I call myself”)!
4. Verbs that change their vowel: e → ie, o → ue
You’ve already seen “querer → quiero”. Several verbs do the same. In the dialogue: empezar (to start) → empiezo. Others change o to ue: acostarse → me acuesto.
The “boot” rule: the change happens in every person except nosotros and vosotros. If you draw the table, the changed forms make the shape of a boot.
“Nunca” at the beginning does NOT need “no”: “Nunca bebo café”. If it comes after the verb, you put “no” before the verb: “No bebo café nunca” (a double negative, which is correct in Spanish).
Pablo, Ana’s brother, works from home as a programmer. Here is his week.
My name is Pablo and I’m a programmer. I work from home, but on Tuesdays I go to the office.
I usually get up at a quarter to eight.
First I have a shower, then I have breakfast with my children: coffee for me, milk for them.
At nine, my wife Elena takes the children to school.
I start work at half past nine and finish at six.
Tuesdays are different: I get up at seven and go to the office by metro.
On Wednesdays and Fridays I go to the gym in the afternoon.
We have dinner at nine in the evening. In Spain we have dinner very late.
Then we watch TV or read a book.
I go to bed at a quarter to twelve. Sometimes at half past twelve.
I never work at the weekend. On Saturdays I rest, and on Sundays we eat with my parents.
My grandmother Rosario always says: “Pablo, you work too much!” And she’s right.

Ana teaches Spanish to foreigners. She works at a language school in the centre of Madrid.
On Mondays, Ana gets up at seven. First she has a shower and gets dressed.
Then she drinks a white coffee and eats toast with tomato. She always listens to the radio while she has breakfast.
At a quarter to eight she leaves home and goes to school by metro.
On the metro she reads a book. At the moment she’s reading a novel by a Mexican writer.
She starts work at nine. In the morning she has two classes: one at A1 level and another at B2 level.
Her students come from many countries: Japan, Brazil, Germany, China…
At two she has lunch with her colleagues in a bar near the school. She usually has the set menu.
In the afternoon she prepares her classes for the next day.
At six she finishes and sometimes goes to the gym. Other times she meets Mihai for a walk in the Retiro.
She has dinner at half past nine, watches a series and goes to bed at a quarter to twelve.
Mondays are long, but Ana loves her job.
